name: Character / mascot treatment
controls: Whether a character or mascot appears, what kind of being it is, how it is drawn, and how it is animated.
question: Should a character or mascot appear, and what kind?
notes: Main options describe the character type and its rendering; the animation facet describes the technique. These combine freely (a blob character can be frame-by-frame or puppet-rigged). 'Mascot' means a recurring brand character; 'character' is any figure acting in the piece. Rendering overlaps with the illustration and material dimensions: a 3D mascot or clay mascot should agree with those choices. Rubber-hose is both a historical drawing style and an animation approach; it is listed as a facet here because it is chiefly about limb motion. In HyperFrames, characters are SVG or layered PNG puppets animated on the GSAP timeline, or Lottie files seeked by the timeline; true frame-by-frame means swapping drawn frames on a stepped schedule. Terms like 'blob character' and 'cursor as character' are informal but widely used in product motion. Choose 'none' to keep the piece character-free; most SaaS product films are.

options.what: No figures or mascots; the product, type and graphics carry the story.
options.looks: UI, typography, shapes and objects only; any human presence is implied (a cursor, a notification).
options.motion: All motion belongs to interface, type and graphic elements.
options.use: Most SaaS launch films, developer tools, premium hardware, data stories.
options.vs: Cursor as character gives the cursor intention and personality; with no character, the cursor is only a pointer.
options.prompt: Use no characters, mascots, hands or human figures. Let the interface, typography and graphic shapes carry all action; any implied user is represented only by a plain system cursor moving efficiently.

options.what: Human figures drawn with naturalistic proportions and anatomy.
options.looks: Correct proportions (7-8 heads tall), detailed faces, clothing folds, shading; illustrated or 3D.
options.motion: Naturalistic acting: weight shifts, walk cycles, lip sync, subtle gestures.
options.use: Narrative brand films, healthcare, HR and people products, testimonial-style explainers.
options.vs: Stylized humans exaggerate proportions and simplify; realistic humans take far more animation effort and risk the uncanny valley in 3D.
options.prompt: Draw human characters with naturalistic proportions (7.5 heads tall), simple but correct anatomy, flat color with one shadow tone, diverse and specific (age, body type, clothing). Animate with weight: ease in and out of poses, 2-3 frame holds, subtle breathing (1-2% chest scale over 3s).

options.what: Human figures with simplified, exaggerated or graphic proportions.
options.looks: Oversized limbs or small heads, simplified faces or dot eyes, flat color, strong silhouettes; the 'corporate Memphis' / Alegria look is one (now overused) variant.
options.motion: Snappy pose-to-pose acting, puppet rigs, exaggerated gestures, looped actions.
options.use: Tech explainers, onboarding, marketing sites, fintech and HR tools.
options.vs: Abstract humans reduce the figure to shapes; stylized humans are still clearly people. 'Corporate Memphis' is a pejorative informal label for one flat stylized-human trend.
refs: Alegria illustration system by Buck for Facebook (2017)
options.prompt: Draw stylized humans with deliberate exaggeration: long limbs, small heads (5-6 heads tall), simple dot or line faces, flat fills in the brand palette, no outlines. Animate pose-to-pose with snappy eases (power3.inOut, 250-400ms) and one expressive gesture per beat.

options.what: A human presence reduced to geometric forms, silhouettes or suggestive shapes.
options.looks: Circles for heads, rectangles or curves for bodies, no facial features; silhouettes and gesture lines.
options.motion: Shape-based motion: bodies assemble from primitives, gestures read through posture alone.
options.use: Data stories, social-impact films, conceptual explainers, premium brands avoiding literal people.
options.vs: Geometric characters are invented beings made of shapes; abstract humans are recognizably human. Faceless characters keep bodies but drop faces.
options.prompt: Represent people as abstract figures: a circle head and a rounded capsule body, no faces or hands, 2-3 flat colors. Convey emotion only through posture and spacing; animate by assembling primitives (scale from 0, stagger 60ms) and tilting the body 5-15 degrees for gesture.

options.what: An amorphous, soft-bodied creature with a simple face and no fixed skeleton.
options.looks: Organic rounded body, dot or bean eyes, minimal mouth, bright flat or soft-gradient fill.
options.motion: Squash and stretch, jiggle, shape morphing between moods, wobbling idle.
options.use: Consumer apps, wellness, kids, playful onboarding and error states.
options.vs: Geometric characters keep hard primitive shapes; blobs morph freely. Clay mascots may be blobs but are rendered as sculpted material.
options.prompt: Design a blob character: soft organic body as one SVG path, two dot eyes (8% of body width), small curved mouth, single saturated fill with a soft highlight. Animate a breathing idle (scaleY 1 to 1.04, scaleX 1 to 0.97 over 1.6s, ease sine.inOut, yoyo) and morph the body path between moods.

options.what: A character built from primitive shapes (circles, squares, triangles) with minimal features.
options.looks: Primitive bodies, simple eyes, flat colors, strict geometry; often a brand shape turned into a being.
options.motion: Rolling, flipping, stacking, rigid rotations, cute hops with small squash.
options.use: Tech brands, abstract explainers, educational content, brand systems derived from a logo shape.
options.vs: Blob characters are soft and morph; geometric characters keep their shapes and move rigidly. Abstract humans are people; geometric characters are invented beings.
options.prompt: Build the character from primitives only: a square or circle body, two circular eyes, no limbs or stick limbs of 6px strokes, flat brand colors. Move it rigidly: roll by rotating 90 degrees per step while translating, hop with 90% scaleY squash on landing.

options.what: An everyday object or product given a face, limbs or personality.
options.looks: The recognizable object with eyes, mouth and sometimes rubber-hose limbs; preserves product silhouette.
options.motion: Object-appropriate motion plus acting: a folder yawns, a coffee cup hops, a card waves.
options.use: Product explainers, food and beverage, file and document tools, ads.
options.conveys: Humor, relatability, making the abstract product personable.
options.vs: Interface-element-as-character keeps the element faceless and gives it behavior; anthropomorphic objects get faces and bodies.
options.prompt: Turn the key object into a character without losing its silhouette: add two oval eyes in the upper third and an optional small mouth, thin stick or rubber-hose limbs only if needed. Act through the object's own mechanics (lids open to speak, pages flap) plus eye blinks every 3-4s.

options.what: A brand character based on an animal, usually stylized and simplified.
options.looks: Recognizable species features simplified to a strong silhouette, big eyes, a signature color.
options.motion: Expressive acting, reactions, celebration loops, walk and run cycles.
options.use: Consumer apps, education, gaming, sports, food brands.
options.vs: Anthropomorphic objects are inanimate things brought to life; animal mascots are creatures by default.
options.prompt: Design an animal mascot with a strong silhouette readable at 120px, oversized head (40% of height), large eyes, one signature brand color, simplified limbs. Animate with appealing acting: anticipation before every action (5-10% counter-motion), follow-through on ears and tail.

options.what: A mechanical or AI character, usually friendly and simplified.
options.looks: Rounded or boxy body, screen or LED eyes, antennae, panel lines, glossy or matte plastic.
options.motion: Mechanical precision mixed with charm: servo-like snaps, head tilts, eye-screen expressions, hovering.
options.use: AI products, automation tools, developer tools, education in tech.
options.vs: Interface-element-as-character keeps the AI invisible behind UI; a robot mascot gives it a body, which can feel dated for serious AI brands.
options.prompt: Design a friendly robot: rounded-rectangle head with a dark screen face showing two pill-shaped glowing eyes, compact body, no mouth. Animate with snappy servo moves (ease power4.inOut, 200ms) plus a 4px hover bob (ease sine.inOut, 2s), expressing emotion by reshaping the eye pills.

options.what: A loosely hand-drawn character with sketchy, imperfect lines.
options.looks: Wobbly marker or pen lines, uneven fills that miss the lines, simple faces, notebook energy.
options.motion: Boiling lines, frame-by-frame at 8-12fps, jerky charming timing.
options.use: Education, creative tools, community content, startup explainers with a casual tone.
options.vs: Hand-drawn icons are the same look at icon scale; sticker mascots are clean and die-cut.
options.prompt: Draw the mascot with 4-6px wobbly black marker lines and flat color fills offset 3-6px from the lines. Animate on twos (hold each pose 2 frames at 24fps) and boil: cycle 3 redrawn versions of the line art every 3 frames even when still.

options.what: A character rendered as a die-cut sticker with a thick white border.
options.looks: Bold flat character art, 8-12px white outline, drop shadow, slight tilt; collectible sticker-pack look.
options.motion: Slap-on entrances, peel-offs, pose swaps like a sticker set, wobble.
options.use: Messaging apps, social content, community brands, merch-driven brands.
options.vs: Doodle mascots are sketchy; sticker mascots are clean and bordered. Sticker icons are the same treatment for icons.
options.prompt: Render the mascot as a die-cut sticker: clean flat art, 10px white border following the silhouette, box-shadow 0 8px 16px rgba(0,0,0,0.2), rotated -6 to 6 degrees. Swap poses as separate stickers slapped on (scale 1.3 to 1 with rotation, 250ms, ease back.out(2.5)).

options.what: A character modeled and rendered in 3D with lighting and materials.
options.looks: Volumetric forms, subsurface or plastic materials, studio lighting, Pixar-adjacent appeal.
options.motion: Full-body acting, secondary motion on appendages, camera moves around the character.
options.use: Premium consumer brand films, gaming, app launches with big budgets.
options.vs: Clay mascots are 3D but matte and handmade-looking; 3D mascots can be glossy and hyper-polished.
options.prompt: Present a 3D mascot with smooth plastic or soft-vinyl materials, three-point studio lighting, soft contact shadow. In HTML, use pre-rendered image sequences or a Three.js/GLB model seeked by the timeline; animate a looped idle plus one hero action per scene with overlapping follow-through.

options.what: A character that looks sculpted from clay or plasticine, stop-motion or 3D-simulated.
options.looks: Matte surfaces, visible fingerprints or tool marks, soft rounded forms, warm lighting.
options.motion: Stop-motion stepping (12fps), squash on contact, slight surface boil between frames.
options.use: Warm consumer brands, food, kids, handcrafted-feeling campaigns.
options.vs: 3D mascots are polished; clay mascots show imperfections. Claymation is the stop-motion technique; 'clay style' 3D imitates it.
options.prompt: Render the mascot as matte clay: soft rounded forms, subtle surface imperfections, warm key light. Animate at 12fps with steps() easing so motion stutters like stop-motion, add 1-2% random scale jitter per frame to imitate hand-repositioning, squash on every contact.

options.what: A body-complete character with no facial features.
options.looks: Full figure with clothing and posture but a blank head; expression carried by gesture.
options.motion: Body-language acting: posture, gesture, walking, pointing; no facial animation needed.
options.use: Inclusive brand illustration, SaaS explainers, stock-style marketing.
options.conveys: Universality, inclusivity, focus on action rather than identity.
options.vs: Abstract humans reduce the body too; faceless characters keep detailed bodies and drop only the face.
options.prompt: Draw characters with full bodies, clothing and hair but blank faces. Carry every emotion through posture: shoulders, head tilt 10-20 degrees, arm gestures. Animate pose-to-pose with clear silhouettes readable in solid black.

options.what: Only hands appear on screen, acting on objects or UI.
options.looks: Illustrated, 3D or photographed hands entering from frame edges, holding, tapping, swiping.
options.motion: Taps, swipes, pinches, holds; hand enters, performs, exits.
options.use: Mobile app demos, how-tos, product interaction explainers, tactile product ads.
options.conveys: Direct interaction, ease of use, human scale.
options.vs: Cursor as character represents desktop interaction; hand-only represents touch. Human characters show the whole person.
options.prompt: Show only a hand (flat illustrated with one shadow tone, or photographic cut-out) entering from the bottom or side edge. Tap: press scales finger 0.95 and triggers a 40px ripple on the UI; swipe: travel 300px in 350ms ease power2.inOut. Exit the frame between actions.

options.what: The mouse cursor behaves with intention and personality, acting as the protagonist.
options.looks: Standard or custom-styled pointer, sometimes with a name tag (multiplayer cursors), trails or expressive motion.
options.motion: Curved, humanlike paths, anticipation before clicks, hesitations, playful wiggles, multiple cursors collaborating.
options.use: Collaboration tools, design tools, SaaS demos, landing-page heroes.
options.vs: A plain cursor is a pointer following a path; cursor as character adds personality (wiggles, names, reactions).
options.prompt: Treat the cursor as the protagonist: move it along curved bezier paths (MotionPathPlugin, 500-900ms, ease power2.inOut) with a 120ms hover pause before each click, click squash to 0.9 scale, and a colored name-tag label; add a second cursor for collaboration beats.

options.what: A UI component (card, button, toggle, chat bubble) behaves like a living character without a face.
options.looks: Real UI elements that stretch, lean, bounce and react with personality.
options.motion: Squash and stretch on UI components, anticipation, reactions to other elements, follow-through on stops.
options.use: Playful SaaS launches, AI assistant reveals, micro-interaction showcases.
options.conveys: Delight, liveliness, a product with personality.
options.vs: Anthropomorphic objects get faces and limbs; interface-as-character stays faceless and expresses through motion alone.
options.prompt: Give one UI component character through motion only: it anticipates (scaleX 0.95, 80ms) before moving, stretches along travel direction (scaleX 1.08) at speed, squashes on landing, and reacts to neighbors with small 3-5 degree tilts. No faces or limbs.

options.what: Key poses are designed first and in-betweens interpolated, giving controlled, readable acting.
options.prompt: Define 3-5 key poses per action; hold each 150-400ms and tween between them in 200-350ms with ease power3.inOut, adding 1-2 breakdown poses for arcs.

options.what: A character built from separate layered parts pinned at joints and rotated (cutout / FK-style).
options.prompt: Split the character into layered SVG parts (head, torso, upper and lower limbs) with transform-origin at each joint; animate by rotating parts in a parent-child hierarchy (forward kinematics), limbs overlapping by 40-80ms.

options.what: Inverse kinematics: animating an end point (hand, foot) and letting the joint chain solve itself.
options.prompt: Animate hand and foot targets and solve the two-bone chain (upper/lower limb) each frame with a simple IK solve so feet stay planted and hands stay on objects; bend direction fixed per limb.

options.what: Every frame (or every other frame) is a separate drawing.
options.prompt: Swap between pre-drawn frames on a stepped schedule (on twos at 24fps = each drawing held 83ms) by toggling visibility on the timeline; no tweening between drawings.

options.what: Limbs as smooth bendy tubes with no elbows or knees, from 1920s-30s cartoons.
options.prompt: Draw limbs as single curved strokes of constant width with round caps; animate by moving the hand/foot end and recomputing the bezier curve so the limb bends in a smooth arc; white-glove hands optional.

options.what: Economical animation: only some parts move, many holds, reused cycles.
options.prompt: Move only what carries meaning (mouth, one arm, eyes); hold everything else; reuse cycles; animate on threes (125ms per drawing) for a deliberate, graphic feel.

options.what: A short seamless gesture cycle (wave, nod, idle breathing) repeated.
options.prompt: Build a 1-2s gesture whose last frame matches the first (yoyo or closed-loop keys), ease sine.inOut, and repeat it a whole number of times within the scene duration.

options.what: The character responds visibly to an event in the scene.
options.prompt: On the triggering event, hold the character for 100ms, then take (anticipation 5%), react with the full pose in 200ms (ease back.out(2)), settle over 300ms.

options.what: Volume-preserving deformation that sells weight and flexibility.
options.prompt: Stretch along motion direction at peak speed (scaleY 1.2, scaleX 0.85), squash on contact (scaleY 0.8, scaleX 1.2), keeping area roughly constant; recover in 150-250ms ease back.out.

options.what: Expressions change through eyes, brows and mouth.
options.prompt: Swap or morph eye and mouth shapes for each expression over 80-150ms; lead with a blink (eyes close 2 frames), brows move 60ms before the mouth.

options.what: Follow-through and overlapping action on appendages (hair, ears, tails, clothing) after the main move.
options.prompt: Delay appendages 60-120ms behind the parent move and overshoot by 10-20 degrees before settling with ease elastic.out(1, 0.5) over 400-600ms.
